open-question.question: How does a run of the on-demand suite name the host it drives (Claude Code, Antigravity, or Codex), and what does a run that names none do? The suite today is bound to Antigravity by module constants: it reads no pytest option or environment variable and parametrizes no test. The two choices are asked together because they constrain each other: a mechanism such as one parametrized case per host already fixes the unnamed run as every host, so not every pairing of mechanism and unnamed-run behaviour is viable.
open-question.alternative: A pytest command-line option (for example `--host claude|antigravity|codex`) that the suite's conftest registers. It takes exactly one host per run. A run that names none stops in the existing `pytest_cmdline_main` hook before any test, with one prerequisite-style stderr line listing the three accepted values and a non-zero exit, never a skip. An unknown value stops the same way. No run drives a host the caller did not name. This matches the plugin's habit of required arguments with no default (`--milestone`, `--at`, the task-list tool's position group). The value is parsed before the prerequisite hook runs, so the hook checks only the named host's CLI and copy, and the exit-1 contract stays as it is. Today's bare command stops instead of running, so every documented invocation (the Commands line in `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, release check g) has to spell out the flag. Covering all three hosts takes three separate runs. How many runs the pre-flight needs depends on the sibling question of which hosts it covers.

The same single-valued pytest option. A run that names none drives Antigravity, the one host the suite drives today, with Antigravity's prerequisite checks. Every existing invocation keeps its current meaning without being edited. A maintainer who only ever ran the Antigravity suite sees no change in behaviour. One host gets a privileged default that the goal does not give it. A bare run quietly covers one host out of three, which leaves the other two unchecked in exactly the setting (an unattended pre-flight, a contributor's habit) where nobody notices. It also keeps the Antigravity binding the milestone is meant to remove, only moved into a default.

A pytest option that may be given once or several times (or take a comma-separated list) to name a subset of hosts. A run that names none drives all three hosts in one session, each test running once per host. Before any test, the prerequisite hook checks every host the run covers and stops on the first one that fails. A single bare command checks what the goal requires, all three tests on all three hosts, while naming one host still narrows a run for development or diagnosis. A bare run fails up front unless every host's CLI and copy pass their checks. On the maintainer's machine as checked on 2026-11-09, the Antigravity and Codex copies are both stale, so the default run cannot start until both are refreshed. A full run is roughly three times as long, with each headless process bounded on the order of 20 minutes. Whether that cost is acceptable depends on the sibling questions about release pre-flight coverage and refreshing installed copies.

A single-valued pytest option. A run that names none drives every host whose CLI resolves on `PATH` (`claude`, `agy`, `codex`), one after another in one session. The full prerequisite checks apply only to the hosts found, and the run stops when it finds none. A contributor with only one of the three CLIs can still run the bare command and get the one host they can check, while the maintainer, who has all three installed, gets full coverage from the same command. Which hosts a bare run covers depends on what happens to be on `PATH`. The same command therefore means different things on different machines, and nothing in its output warns when a host was left out because its CLI was missing. On the maintainer's machine it behaves exactly like running all three, stale-copy stop included.

An environment variable (for example `CAIRN_SUITE_HOST`) that the prerequisite hook reads, naming exactly one host. When it is unset or empty the run stops before any test with one prerequisite-style line listing the accepted values, and an unknown value stops the same way. The suite registers no pytest option. Set once in a shell or a CI step, it carries across every later `uv run pytest` call and through any wrapper that does not forward pytest arguments, and adding it needs no pytest option registration. The run's command line no longer shows which host it drove, so a log or a pasted command loses that fact. A value left over in the shell picks the host silently on later runs: the per-shell state the plugin's milestone addressing turned down for `--milestone` in favour of a typed path on every call.

An environment variable naming exactly one host. When it is unset, the run drives Antigravity, as the suite does today. No pytest option is registered. This is the smallest change to how the suite is invoked: nothing documented has to change, and choosing another host means adding one variable before the command. It combines a privileged Antigravity default with a choice that is invisible on the command line. A forgotten or stale variable, or its absence, decides the host without any sign in the command. A bare run covers one host out of three.

alternative.id: Host environment variable, unnamed runs all

open-question.alternative: An environment variable that may name one host or a comma-separated subset. When it is unset, the run drives all three hosts in one session, and before any test the prerequisite hook checks every host the run covers. The bare command gives full coverage, and a shell or CI step can narrow every run to one host once, without repeating a flag. It shares the all-hosts default's costs: a bare run that cannot start while any copy is stale (both are stale on the maintainer's machine today), and roughly three times the run time. It adds the environment variable's costs too: the narrowing is invisible in the command, and a leftover value silently narrows later runs.

alternative.id: Host environment variable, unnamed runs installed

open-question.alternative: An environment variable naming exactly one host. When it is unset, the run drives every host whose CLI resolves on `PATH`, one after another in one session, with the full prerequisite checks applied to those hosts and a stop when none is found. A bare run adapts to the machine, and a shell that has settled on one host keeps using it, with no flag on any command. Neither the command nor the shell's visible state reliably says which hosts a run covered. That depends both on `PATH` and on a variable that may be left over, so two identical commands can test different hosts with nothing in the output to say so.

alternative.id: Parametrized per host, unnamed runs all

open-question.alternative: Each test is parametrized over the three hosts, one test case per host with the host as its id, and a run chooses hosts through pytest's own selection (`-k codex`, or a per-host marker with `-m`). It needs no option or variable of the suite's own. A run that selects nothing runs every case, so it covers all three hosts. Because selection is known only after collection, the prerequisite check either runs for all three hosts in `pytest_cmdline_main`, or moves to a collection-time hook that checks only the hosts whose cases were selected. Selection uses standard pytest tooling with nothing invented, and each host's result appears as its own named test outcome. One run's report therefore shows per host which test passed or failed, which suits the goal's "pass against all three hosts". Selecting hosts with `-k` matches substrings and can pick up unintended cases. The prerequisite hook either loses the before-collection, one-line, exit-1 stop for a selected host (when it moves to a collection hook) or refuses a single-host run because some unselected host's copy is stale (when it checks all three). A bare run has the all-hosts costs: it cannot start while any copy is stale, and it takes about three times as long.

Each test is parametrized over the three hosts and selected through `-k`/`-m`, as above. A host whose CLI is missing from `PATH` has its cases skipped with a reason that names it, while the hosts that are present get the full prerequisite checks and stop the run on a failure. A run that selects nothing therefore covers every installed host. The suite runs on any contributor's machine with any subset of the CLIs, and every case left out still shows in the report as a named skip rather than disappearing. It rejects the suite's settled contract that a missing prerequisite stops the run and is never a skip. An unattended pre-flight can then pass with a host's tests all skipped, which is exactly the silent gap that contract exists to prevent. It also carries the parametrized form's `-k` substring matching and its split prerequisite timing.

open-question.question: How does the suite find the installed plugin copy of Claude Code and of Codex, whose host definitions record no install path? Antigravity's copy sits at the fixed global path ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, held as a suite constant. On the maintainer's machine Claude Code loads the plugin straight from this checkout's hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, with versioned copies also under ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/, and Codex copies it at install time to a versioned directory under ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/.
open-question.alternative: The suite uses one fixed location per host, just as it already does for Antigravity. For Claude Code that location is this checkout's hosts/claude/, the folder the directory marketplace reads from. For Codex it is ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/<VERSION>/, where <VERSION> is read from the checkout's VERSION file. The host CLI is never asked, and no per-run value is taken. It is the simplest rule and matches the existing Antigravity constant. Locating a copy needs no output parsing, depends on no CLI version, and is one path join per host. A Codex copy installed at the version being built is exactly the copy this rule finds. A Codex copy installed under any other version, such as today's 1.7.6 against a 1.9.0 checkout, reads as no copy at all rather than as a stale one. The Claude Code path holds only for a directory-marketplace install: a copy installed from the distribution repository lives in the versioned cache, so the suite would check and assert against a folder claude does not load. Nothing confirms that the run in the seeded repository loads the folder named.

For Claude Code the location is fixed at this checkout's hosts/claude/. For Codex the suite takes ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/ as a fixed parent and uses the version directory it finds there: the only one, or the newest by version when there are several. When there is none, the prerequisite stops the run. The host CLI is never asked, and no per-run value is taken. A Codex copy at any installed version is found. A stale install such as today's 1.7.6 then reaches the freshness check and is reported as out of date, not as missing, which points the user at the real remedy. The rule still needs no CLI output parsing. "Newest directory" is only a guess at the copy Codex loads. A leftover version directory that a later install left behind, or an older version re-installed, would be picked up silently. The Claude Code half has the same limit as the checkout-version rule: it is right only for a directory-marketplace install. How much a wrong pick matters depends on what the freshness sibling requires of the copy.

Both hosts are located by one uniform rule: the host's versioned plugin cache at the checkout's VERSION. That is ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/<VERSION>/ for Claude Code and ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/<VERSION>/ for Codex. The checkout's hosts/claude/ is never treated as the installed copy, the host CLI is never asked, and no per-run value is taken. One rule covers both hosts, and it describes a real install as a user gets it from a marketplace. The suite therefore checks the kind of copy a distribution-repository user runs, not the maintainer's live checkout. On the maintainer's machine claude reads cairn from hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, at user scope too. The cache copy at 1.9.0 would then be compared and asserted against while the run actually loads a different folder, so the suite could pass or fail for a copy no test used. Codex installed at any version other than the checkout's reads as absent.

Before any test, the suite asks each host's own CLI where the installed copy is. For Claude Code it runs claude plugin list --json and takes the cairn@cairn entry for the scope that applies to a repository outside any recorded project: its readFromFolder when set, otherwise its installPath. For Codex it runs codex plugin list, takes the installed cairn@cairn version, and builds ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/<version>/ from it. Where the CLI reports no install, the prerequisite stops the run. No per-run value is taken. It finds the copy the host itself says it loads, whatever the install form. For Claude Code that is today's folder-read checkout, a cache copy after a distribution-repository install, or a changed scope. For Codex a stale install is found at its real version and reported as stale. The suite comes to depend on CLI output that the repository has neither described nor pinned. claude's JSON fields and codex's text table may change across CLI versions and break the prerequisite with no test of their own. codex plugin list prints the marketplace source, not the cache path, so the Codex half still rests on the cache-layout convention. Neither host's hands-on block covers these listings.

The installed root for Claude Code and for Codex is supplied by whoever runs the suite, as one per-run value such as a pytest option or an environment variable. Antigravity keeps its fixed constant. A run against Claude Code or Codex that names no root stops on the prerequisite line, with a remedy naming the value to set. The suite never guesses a location and never asks the CLI. The suite holds no assumption about install layout or CLI output that could go stale. The person running it states the copy they mean, which covers any install form, including an unusual one. Every run on those two hosts needs an extra value that the person must look up. The suite also trusts that value: a path to a copy the host does not actually load is checked and asserted against without complaint. The release pre-flight, which runs the suite unattended, would have to carry the path, and the per-run invocation gets longer. How the value is spelled per run also relates to the host-selection sibling's mechanism.

The installed root is an optional per-run value, such as a pytest option or an environment variable, available on every host. When it is absent, each host falls back to a fixed default: Antigravity's ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, this checkout's hosts/claude/ for Claude Code, and the version directory found under ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/ for Codex. A typical run needs no extra value on any host. Any install the default misses, such as a distribution-repository Claude Code install or a second Codex version, can still be named without changing the suite. It carries both a convention to keep current and an override to document and test. A default that is wrong for the person running the suite still checks the wrong copy silently unless they know to override it. The override's spelling relates to the host-selection sibling's mechanism.

For Claude Code the suite starts claude with --plugin-dir pointing at this checkout's hosts/claude/, so the session loads the built tree and no installed copy has to be located. For Codex, which lists no option to load a plugin for one session only, the copy is located at ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/<VERSION>/ from the checkout's VERSION file. No per-run value is taken. On Claude Code the plugin under test is by construction the tree just built. That removes both the location question and any staleness for that host, and it needs no install step before a run. It departs from the goal's wording, which says the suite drives each host's installed plugin copy, so on Claude Code it tests the build rather than the install. A user-scope cairn@cairn that is already enabled could load beside the --plugin-dir copy and make it ambiguous which one ran. Codex is left with the checkout-version rule's limits, so the two hosts are treated unevenly.

The suite does not locate the Claude Code or Codex copy before a run. Each test learns the root the host actually resolved from that run's own tool-call records, taken as the directory above the first file read under a shared/ path, and makes its root-relative assertions against it. No prerequisite check names a location for those two hosts. Whatever copy the host loaded is the one the assertions use, with no layout convention, CLI listing, or per-run value to maintain. The plugin-root test's assertion that reads land under the installed root becomes circular, because the root is taken from those same reads. The suite also has no copy to compare before any test runs. This option works only if the freshness sibling requires nothing of the copy and the tool-call-record sibling keeps a parsable record of file reads on both hosts.

open-question.question: What must the prerequisite check require of the chosen host's installed plugin copy before any test runs? For Antigravity it requires the copy to be byte-identical, file for file, to the committed built tree hosts/antigravity/. On Claude Code the plugin can be loaded directly from this checkout's hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, where that comparison holds trivially, and on Codex the copy is a snapshot of hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ taken at install time under the version it was installed at.
open-question.alternative: The existing third prerequisite becomes the rule for all three hosts. The copy the chosen host actually loads must match that host's plugin directory in the committed built tree file for file, a missing or extra file included: hosts/claude/ for Claude Code, hosts/antigravity/ for Antigravity, hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ for Codex. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. When Claude Code loads straight from this checkout's hosts/claude, the comparison passes trivially and is still made. One rule for every host, generalized from the check that already exists. It is the only check here that catches a stale copy carrying the current version number, which is the state found on 2026-11-09: the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees (both still hold shared/get-current-milestone.md and lack shared/resolve-milestone.md). Any file the host adds or rewrites at install time fails it. Nobody has checked whether codex plugin add copies hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ verbatim. On Claude Code the check tells nothing new when the loaded copy is the checkout itself, and it means something only if the located copy is the one the CLI really loads. That depends on how the sibling question on installed copy location settles.

On Antigravity and Codex the installed copy must be byte-identical to the host's built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. On Claude Code the check compares no file contents. It requires instead that the plugin source the CLI reports for cairn@cairn is this checkout's hosts/claude, loaded through the directory marketplace, and it stops the run on any other source, a cached or published copy included, even one byte-identical to the built tree. Every failure stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. On Claude Code the check becomes one that can fail for a real reason: a load from the ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/ copies (the 1.9.0 one is stale) or from the published marketplace. A file comparison that always passes is replaced. Claude Code never needs a reinstall after a core/ change, because the checkout is what loads. Running the suite on Claude Code needs this checkout's directory marketplace. A contributor who installed from the published cairn-claude repository is refused even when that copy is identical. Two different kinds of check now sit behind one prerequisite line, and the Claude Code one relies on reading the plugin source from claude's own report. Whether that report is the right source depends on the sibling question on installed copy location.

On every host the comparison is limited to the plugin's four runtime directories (agents/, shared/, skills/, tools/). Within those directories the installed copy must be byte-identical to the built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. Files outside them are not compared: the manifest directory, README and other top-level files, and any metadata the host adds at install time. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. It still catches every stale skill, procedure, agent, or tool that the tests actually exercise, including a same-version stale copy. It also tolerates whatever a host writes beside the plugin at install time or rewrites in its manifest, which on Codex has not been checked hands-on. It is weaker than the full-tree rule that exists today: a stale or wrong manifest passes unseen, even though the host reads the manifest to load the plugin. The four-directory set becomes one more rule the suite holds, and it must be kept in step with the build's [layout] mapping if a fifth runtime directory is ever added.

On every host the check compares only the version: the version recorded in the installed copy's manifest, or the version the host's own plugin listing reports, must equal VERSION. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. File contents are not compared. It is the cheapest check and the most robust one. It reads one value through each host's own manifest or listing, so it does not depend on which files a host copies or adds at install time, and it catches the Codex 1.7.6 copy at once. VERSION changes only at a release, and the suite runs on unreleased changes. A stale copy at the current version passes: on 2026-11-09 the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees. The suite would then certify old text as working, and it would lose the protection the current Antigravity check gives.

On every host the installed copy is compared byte for byte, file for file, with the host's built plugin directory, as in the full-tree rule. A mismatch prints one line naming the first differing file, and the tests then run anyway against the installed copy. Only a missing CLI or a missing copy still stops the run. The suite can be run on purpose against a copy other than the built tree, such as a published release being checked after the fact or a hand-patched copy under investigation. The run still says plainly that the copy differs. It breaks the suite's convention that a prerequisite stops the run before any test and is never a skip. A pass against a stale copy then means as much as a pass against a fresh one to anything that reads only the outcome, including the release pre-flight's check g, which runs the suite and reads its result.

No host's installed copy is compared against anything. The prerequisite check keeps only that the host's CLI resolves on PATH and that an installed copy is present, and it drops the existing Antigravity byte comparison. Tests run against whatever copy is installed. It needs no per-host comparison logic and no knowledge of what each host's install leaves on disk. It never blocks a run over a difference in a file the tests do not touch. The suite exists to check the committed integration before it is committed or released. Without a freshness check it can pass on a copy that does not contain the change under test, or fail for reasons already fixed, and nothing reports which happened. It also removes a guard that already works for Antigravity.

open-question.question: Which of the assertions that read the host's own tool-call records do the tests keep on all three hosts? Today the plugin-root test reads Antigravity's stream-json records to assert that no agent was dispatched, that a file read under the installed root's shared/ directory completed, and that a shell call running task_list.py insert under that root completed; each dispatch test reads them to assert exactly one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt and no write or shell tool used by the dispatching process. Claude Code (--output-format stream-json) and Codex (codex exec --json) emit records of other shapes that the repository holds no parser for, and every other assertion of the three tests reads only files and git state.

What becomes of the plugin-root test's assertion that every file read attempted with a ~ path ended in ERROR, given that every test of the host-generic suite is to check behaviour that is the same on every host? The assertion pins that Antigravity's file-reading tool refuses the tilde literal its tree renders as the plugin root; the Claude Code and Codex trees render the root as a variable the host resolves, so no tilde path arises there.
open-question.alternative: The assertion that every read attempted with a ~ path ended in ERROR is removed from the plugin-root test outright, with no replacement assertion and no host-specific branch. The test keeps whatever host-neutral checks remain (the shared procedure reached at the expanded root, the task-list insert under the root, the two sections in the seeded list). Antigravity's tilde-refusal behaviour stays recorded only in the dated hands-on block of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml, which no automated run re-checks. Simplest and fully consistent with the goal: the test asserts only what holds on every host, nothing in it needs to know which host it drives, and no per-host value is added to the suite for this one check. The early-warning signal the pin was written for is lost: if a later agy accepts tilde reads, nothing fails, and the settings.toml statement that the file-reading tool refuses the tilde form can go stale silently until someone re-checks by hand.

The pin is replaced by one host-neutral assertion run identically on every host: every file read in the host's records that ended DONE carried an absolute path. No per-host value is used; on Antigravity a DONE tilde read is not absolute and so still fails the test, while on Claude Code and Codex, whose rendered root arrives resolved, the assertion holds without any tilde arising. Keeps the Antigravity pin's failure signal (a tilde read ending DONE fails exactly as before) while stating a property that is the same on every host, so the test body needs no host branch and the goal's every-test-is-host-generic rule holds. It is stricter than the pin: any host whose read tool accepts a relative path, or a run that legitimately reads a workspace file by a relative path, fails the test though nothing is wrong with plugin-root resolution. It needs file-read records parsed on every host, including Codex, which may read through shell commands rather than a read tool; that depends on which record assertions the tests keep on all three hosts, a sibling question.

The pin is generalized into one assertion of the same shape on every host, parametrized by that host's rendered plugin-root literal as its definition's plugin_root declares it (~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, ${PLUGIN_ROOT}): every file read attempted with that unexpanded literal ended in ERROR. Reads of other paths are not constrained. Preserves the pin's exact meaning on Antigravity, scoped to plugin-root reads only, while one assertion shape runs on all three hosts; taking the literal from the host definition keeps it tied to what the build actually renders. On Claude Code and Codex the assertion is vacuous in practice, since their root arrives resolved and no unexpanded read arises, so it is host-generic in form rather than in what it checks. It adds a per-host value the suite must read, whose home is a sibling question, and needs read records parsed on every host, which the sibling question on kept record assertions decides.

The assertion stays inside the plugin-root test unchanged but runs only when the run drives Antigravity, skipped silently on the other two hosts, reusing the same headless run. This rejects the goal's premise that every test checks only behaviour the same on every host, so the goal would need revising to admit host-conditional assertions. Keeps the pin exactly as it is, with its signal intact and no extra headless run, at the cost of one conditional line. Contradicts the recorded goal and opens the door to host branches inside generic tests, the pattern the milestone exists to remove. It depends on the test knowing which host the run drives, which the host-selection sibling question settles.

The pin moves out of the plugin-root test into its own test, collected only when the run drives Antigravity and skipped or deselected on the other hosts, with its own headless agy run of a skill that reads a shared procedure. The plugin-root test itself becomes host-generic; this still rejects the goal's premise that every test in the suite is host-generic, so the goal would need revising to admit one declared host-specific test. Keeps the pin and its early-warning signal while leaving every shared test body free of host branches, and the exception is visible by name in the test report rather than buried in a conditional. Costs an extra headless Antigravity run (bounded only by agy's 20-minute print timeout) to re-establish what the plugin-root run already shows, and still contradicts the recorded goal. It depends on how a run names its host, which the host-selection sibling question settles.

open-question.question: How do the two agent-dispatch tests get their agent dispatched on each host? Today each test's own prompt tells the headless process to call Antigravity's invoke_subagent with the agent's bare name and the real three-line dispatch prompt, so no orchestrator skill stands between the test and the agent. Claude Code dispatches through its Agent tool by the namespaced name cairn:<agent>, and Codex registers no agent name: its orchestrators start a generic subagent whose prompt opens by telling it to read the plugin's agent file under the installed root.
open-question.alternative: Each test keeps a dispatching process of its own with no orchestrator skill between it and the agent, and its prompt names the host's own dispatch mechanism, authored as one per-host value set: on Claude Code the Agent tool with subagent_type cairn:<agent>, on Antigravity invoke_subagent with the bare name as TypeName (as today), and on Codex spawn_agent starting a generic subagent. The prompt handed over is the host's real dispatch prompt: the three-line prompt alone on Claude Code and Antigravity, and on Codex that prompt opened by the line its *_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS slot renders, naming the agent file under the installed root. The pass signals stay the files the agent lands, unchanged. It keeps exactly what the tests isolate today, the agent's own contract under the host's real dispatch path with the dispatched agent's tool grant exercised, so a failure points at the agent or its dispatch and not at an orchestrator, and every file-based assertion carries over to all three hosts untouched. The suite holds a hand-written copy of each host's dispatch wording that can drift from the shipped slot values, and on Codex the prompt must name the agent file by its expanded installed path because the test prompt is not skill text the host resolves ${PLUGIN_ROOT} in; it depends on how the sibling questions on the installed copy's location, on where per-host values live, and on which tool-call record assertions are kept settle.

Each test keeps its own dispatching process with no orchestrator skill between, but composes the dispatch instruction from the built tree of the host under test rather than from wording the suite authors: it reads the dispatch paragraph and the prompt fence the host's rendered complete-all-tasks and provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions skills carry (the filled ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH, COMPLETE_TASK_DISPATCH, and *_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS slots), substitutes the Short Title or task name, the seeded milestone directory, the scratch directory, and on Codex the installed root, and hands that text to the process. The pass signals stay the files the agent lands, unchanged. The test drives the dispatch wording the plugin actually ships on each host, so a slot value that no longer dispatches on its host fails the suite, and no second copy of that wording exists in the suite to drift. Pulling a paragraph and a fence out of rendered skill prose is a parser over runtime text that was written for a runner, not a test, so a rewording of the surrounding step can break the extraction, and the extracted paragraph carries orchestrator-only context (sub-step references, per-question fan-out, repair and wait wording) the test must strip or tolerate; on Codex it still needs the expanded installed root, which depends on the sibling question on the installed copy's location.

Each test keeps its own dispatching process with no orchestrator skill between, and one prompt serves every host: it asks the process to dispatch the cairn plugin's named agent as a subagent by whatever means the host has, naming the agent by its bare name and the path of its agent file under the installed root, with the three-line dispatch prompt below it, and names no tool or agent identifier. The pass signals stay the files the agent lands, unchanged. The test text is identical on all three hosts, so the suite carries no per-host dispatch values at all and adding a host adds nothing to these two tests. open-question.question: When a suite test fails on a host because of the plugin's integration for that host and not because of the suite, is fixing the plugin (a slot value, a host definition, or a file under core/) part of this milestone? The goal requires the three existing tests to pass against all three hosts, and no automated test has driven claude or codex before.
open-question.alternative: Fixing the plugin is in scope on every surface the defect needs: a slot value or any other file of the host's definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/, a runtime file under core/ (skills, agents, shared procedures), a tool under core/tools/, or scripts/build_hosts.py. Each fix lands in this milestone as its own task, with the host trees rebuilt and committed with it, so no out-of-scope handling is needed and no test is marked or left failing. The goal's requirement that the three tests pass against all three hosts stays reachable exactly as written, and the first automated drive of claude and codex is the run most likely to surface integration defects, so they are fixed by the milestone that found them while its context is held rather than handed to a later one. The milestone's size is unbounded until the suite has run: a defect in shared runtime prose or a tool changes the rendered trees of every host, owing re-runs on the hosts already passing, the Python suite at both interpreters for a tool change, and possibly a CLAUDE.md invariant edit, so a suite milestone can grow into an integration rework, and with the milestone holding the root scope once started, no other milestone can enter tasks while it does.

Fixing the plugin is in scope only within the failing host's own definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/ (a slot value, settings.toml, or a host template), rebuilt into that host's tree. A defect that needs a change under core/, a tool, or the build script is out of scope: the affected test carries a per-host expected-failure marker in the suite naming the defect, and the fix is left to a later milestone. Host-local fixes change only the one host's rendered tree, so they cannot regress the hosts already passing, the scope stays bounded, and the suite still gives a clean run that the release pre-flight can use as its gate while a core defect waits. A per-host marker is a test that differs by host, which the goal's sentence that only the prerequisite check and the invocation differ rules out, so it needs a goal revision; the marker can outlive its defect if nothing removes it; and every failure needs a judgment of whether its fix is host-local or core before the right branch is known.

alternative.id: Host-local fixes, core defects left failing

open-question.alternative: Fixing the plugin is in scope only within the failing host's own definition under scripts/hosts/<host>/ (a slot value, settings.toml, or a host template), rebuilt into that host's tree. A defect that needs a change under core/, a tool, or the build script is out of scope and is left as it is: the test stays failing on that host with nothing in the suite marking it, the defect is recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope and in its finish summary, and the fix is left to a later milestone, started once this one is finished. The scope stays bounded to suite work and host-local wording, and the suite keeps no host-specific test logic at all, so every test stays exactly one behaviour on every host and the failure stays visible on every run until the fix lands. The milestone finishes with its goal's pass on all three hosts unmet, which needs a goal revision, and a red test on a host blocks the release pre-flight's suite check on every change to its trigger paths until the later milestone lands, so the cost of the deferred defect falls on each release in between.

Fixing the plugin is not part of this milestone on any surface: the milestone changes only the suite and the references to it. Every failure judged an integration defect gets a per-host expected-failure marker in the suite naming the defect, and every fix is left to a later milestone. The milestone stays exactly a test-suite milestone with a size known in advance, no runtime file or host tree changes under it, and the suite still runs clean enough to serve the release pre-flight while each defect it found is documented in the test that found it. Even a one-line slot fix is deferred to a separate milestone, which cannot enter tasks while this root-scoped one is started, and the per-host markers contradict the goal's sentence that only the prerequisite check and invocation differ, so it needs a goal revision; the classification of a failure as a plugin defect rather than a suite defect, judged without fixing anything, is easy to get wrong.

Fixing the plugin is not part of this milestone on any surface: the milestone changes only the suite and the references to it. A test that fails on a host for an integration defect is left failing with nothing in the suite marking it, the defect is recorded under the milestone's Out of Scope and in its finish summary, and every fix is left to a later milestone, started once this one is finished. The milestone's scope is the narrowest possible and the suite stays strictly host-generic, its failures an honest report of where the plugin's integrations stand, handed to a later milestone as found. The goal's pass on all three hosts is given up wholesale and needs a goal revision, the sibling milestone starting-state-refresh, which expects a test of this suite to pass on all three hosts, inherits a red suite, and the release pre-flight's suite check fails until every deferred defect is fixed.
